claims.text: An actively trained moment tensor potential or similar ML interatomic potential can reproduce the free-energy landscapes of solid FCC aluminum and molten aluminum.
The ML potential can retain the vibrational-entropy contribution to aluminum phase free energies.
The ML potential can retain anharmonic contributions to aluminum phase free energies.
The ML potential can retain electron–vibration coupling effects.
The proposed ML workflow will be approximately 10–100 times faster than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD.
The relevant aluminum temperature interval is approximately 900–1100 K and spans the fusion region.
Vibrational fluctuations and electron–vibration coupling are significant for aluminum over approximately 900–1100 K.
Active learning can generate property- and system-specific MLIP training sets while reducing the required amount of DFT data.
Densely sampling configurations near aluminum's phase transition will ensure accurate treatment of vibrational effects.
Densely sampling configurations near aluminum's phase transition will ensure accurate treatment of electron–vibration effects.
Training data should include equilibrated solid and molten aluminum configurations, with emphasis on the melting region.
Local atomic environments and vibrational displacement correlations, including pairwise covariances, mediate phase free-energy differences.
Learning the ab initio energy landscape with an ML potential avoids the need to conduct production sampling using expensive ab initio molecular dynamics.
Focused sampling near fusion improves the capture of electron–vibration coupling that is critical for accurate free-energy differences.
The proposed workflow will predict fusion free energy, latent heat, and entropic contributions within approximately 5% of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The proposed scope is primarily elemental FCC aluminum near its melting point.
Extension of the method to multicomponent systems requires additional validation.
ML-potential accuracy depends on whether the training set adequately covers the relevant configurational space.
A displacement-covariance-based treatment has previously been applied to FCC aluminum and compared with standard thermodynamic data.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD directly include full vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration contributions.
